content: Buchnera aphidicola, a member of the Proteobacteria, serves as the primary endosymbiont of aphids, specifically Acyrthosiphon pisum. It is hypothesized that Buchnera evolved from a free-living gram-negative ancestor, resembling modern Enterobacteriaceae such as Escherichia coli. These bacteria are approximately 3 micrometers in diameter and retain some key characteristics of their Enterobacteriaceae relatives, including a gram-negative cell wall. However, unlike most gram-negative bacteria, Buchnera lacks the genes necessary for the production of lipopolysaccharides (LPS) in their outer membrane. Due to their long-standing association with aphids and the restriction of genetic exchange events caused by strictly vertical transmission, Buchnera has undergone significant gene loss. This includes the deletion of genes required for anaerobic respiration, as well as the synthesis of amino-sugars, fatty acids, phospholipids, and complex carbohydrates. As a result, Buchnera possesses one of the smallest known genomes of any living organism, which is also remarkably genetically stable. The symbiotic relationship between Buchnera and aphids began approximately 150 to 200 million years ago and has been maintained through maternal transmission and co-speciation. Aphids have developed specialized cells, known as bacteriocytes, to house Buchnera. Each aphid contains approximately 6 million Buchnera individuals. Within these bacteriocytes, Buchnera resides in multiple vesicles called symbiosomes, which are derived from the plasma membrane. Buchnera has lost regulatory factors, leading to the continuous overproduction of tryptophan and other amino acids. This overproduction is critical for the nutritional needs of the aphid host, as aphids rely on Buchnera to synthesize essential amino acids that are deficient in their plant sap diet. The genus Buchnera was first named by Paul Baumann and his graduate student. Baumann also conducted the first molecular characterization of a symbiotic bacterium using Buchnera as a model. These initial studies on Buchnera paved the way for broader investigations into the symbionts of various insect groups. Researchers such as Paul and Linda Baumann, Nancy Moran, Serap Aksoy, and Roy Gross expanded this field by studying symbionts in aphids, tsetse flies, ants, leafhoppers, mealybugs, whiteflies, psyllids, and other insects.
